title: 3 Maccabees
subtitle: a king turned back from the Holy of Holies, and elephants turned against their masters
lead: 3 Maccabees is a short Greek story about the Jews of Egypt. Ptolemy IV Philopator, the Greek king of Egypt, beats Antiochus III at Raphia in 217 BC, tours the cities he has won, and comes to Jerusalem. There he decides to go into the sanctuary, though they tell him that only "the high priest, who leads them all, and he only one time each year" may enter (1:11). The city cries out, the high priest Simon prays, and God shakes the king "like a reed in the wind" until he lies helpless on the floor (2:22). Back in Egypt the king takes revenge: Jews must sacrifice, be registered as slaves and branded with the ivy leaf of the god Dionysus, unless they join his mystery rites (2:28-30). Then he orders the Jews of the countryside brought to the hippodrome of Alexandria to be trampled by five hundred elephants drunk on wine and incense (4-5). Three times the plan fails: the king oversleeps, then forgets, and at last, as the old priest Eleazar prays, two angels come down from heaven and the elephants turn on the king's own army (6:16-21). The king repents, throws a seven-day feast, writes a letter of protection, and the Jews found a yearly festival (6:30-7:23). It has 7 chapters and 228 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. Despite its name, the book has nothing to do with Judas Maccabeus or his brothers: it is set about fifty years before their revolt, in Egypt. The Eastern Orthodox churches read it in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint, among the books outside the Hebrew Bible; the Apostolic Canons already count "of the Maccabees, three." It is not in the Catholic Bible or the Protestant Bible, it is not in the Jewish Bible, and the Coptic Orthodox Church does not count it as canonical. Most scholars read it as a work of Alexandrian Jewish literature written in Greek in the last century BC or a little later, a story built around real names and places, and a window on how Jews in Egypt lived as loyal subjects of a pagan king while holding to their God, their Temple and their Law.
facts: The Eastern Orthodox churches (the Apostolic Canons, canon 85, list "of the Maccabees, three"; the Greek and Russian Bibles include it among the books outside the Hebrew canon), and it stands in the Bibles of some other Eastern churches (the Syriac and Armenian). Not Scripture for the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches (whose Meqabyan are other books), the Catholic Church, Protestants or Judaism.
Unknown: a Greek-speaking Jew, almost certainly of Alexandria, who knew the Ptolemaic court's official language well.

Debated. Late Ptolemaic, about 100 to 30 BC (C. W. Emmet put it about 100 BC and Thackeray about 80 BC; also Elias Bickerman, Hugh Anderson, Sara Raup Johnson); early Roman, about 25 to 15 BC, because of the census of the Jews (Victor Tcherikover, Moses Hadas); or the reign of Caligula, about AD 40 (Heinrich Ewald and others). It must be older than the Temple's fall in AD 70.
Raphia near Gaza, Jerusalem and its Temple, then Alexandria and the Egyptian countryside, in the reign of Ptolemy IV Philopator, after the battle of Raphia (217 BC).
Alexandria in Egypt, by almost every view.
Greek, in an ornate, wordy style full of rare words; it was never in Hebrew.

Greek, in Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD) and a few later manuscripts, some with a Lucianic text. Codex Vaticanus has no books of Maccabees, and Codex Sinaiticus passes from 1 Maccabees to 4 Maccabees. A free Syriac version and an Armenian version. There is no Latin version.

A historical tale (scholars also call it a historical romance or novel), with prayers (2:2-20; 6:2-15), two royal letters (3:12-29; 7:1-9), a royal inscription (2:28-30) and the founding of a festival (6:36; 7:19).
7 chapters, 228 verses. Swete's printed Greek has no verse 2:1; the Plain gives it from Brenton's English (see the note there).
authorship: The book names no author. Early Christian lists simply count it among the books of Maccabees (Apostolic Canons 85; the Stichometry of Nicephorus), and Theodoret, as Emmet reports, summarized it in his commentary on Daniel 11 and treated it as history. Christian readers did not claim an ancient prophet or a famous name for it.

An Alexandrian Jew wrote it in Greek. C. W. Emmet (1913) found its official and court words confirmed by Ptolemaic papyri, close links in style and ideas with 2 Maccabees and the Letter of Aristeas ("of school and thought," not copying), and an apparent use of the Greek Song of the Three Young Men in 6:6; he dated it about 100 BC. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) judged it "a very weak piece of fiction" written by an Alexandrian Jew, no earlier than the first century BC. Victor Tcherikover (1945) argued that it is not a true source for the events it tells, but a good source for the time it was written, which its word for the census (laographia) places under Augustus.

Emmet thought the writer joined two stories: a tradition about Philopator at the Temple after Raphia, and a story of elephants loosed on the Jews of Alexandria that Josephus tells about a later king, Ptolemy Physcon (Against Apion 2.53-55). Some, such as Ewald and Grimm, thought the opening was lost, since the book begins with "But Philopator" in the Greek and speaks of Theodotus's plot and the king's "drinking partners and companions already mentioned" (2:25) as if known. Emmet answered that these are traces of a source the writer used, not of a lost beginning.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, above all of Alexandria, in the late Ptolemaic or early Roman period. They lived as a large, settled minority, many of them in the king's service as soldiers, loyal to the king, proud of their Temple far away in Jerusalem, and under steady pressure: neighbors mocked their food laws and their refusal to share in pagan worship (3:4-7), and the city offered rank and citizenship to those who would give way (2:30-31; 3:21). The book's heroes are ordinary Jews of the countryside and two old priests; its villains are a drunken king and his courtiers, and its traitors are Jews who gave up the Law "for the sake of their stomachs" (7:11).
audience.why: It answers the question of every minority under a pagan state: can we stay loyal to the king and to God at once, and will God protect us if we do? The writer insists on both. The Jews "stayed well disposed toward the kings and kept faith with them without wavering" (3:3), and in the end the king himself confesses that "the God of heaven shields the Jews and always fights on their side, as a father for his sons" (7:6). God protects his Temple (1-2) and his people far from it (5-6), through prayer, sleep, forgetting and angels, "the unconquerable providence" (4:21). The book also explains a festival the Egyptian Jews kept (6:36; 7:19) and draws a hard line against those who traded the Law for privilege (2:31-33; 7:10-15). Knowing the readers changes the reading: the story is less a record of one king's reign than a mirror for a community, telling it that faithfulness, not citizenship bought with apostasy, is the safe road.
views: Many readers, Emmet among them, take the book as the founding legend of a feast kept by Egyptian Jews, like Purim in Esther (6:36; 7:19). Emmet thought it may have been read aloud at the festival. Josephus also knew of a day the Alexandrian Jews kept for their rescue from elephants (Against Apion 2.55).
An apology to outsiders as well

Emmet read it as written mainly for Jews, to strengthen their faith, but also for outsiders: it presents the Jew as the Ptolemies' most loyal subject and hints that it is unwise to meddle with his religion.

Tcherikover and Moses Hadas read the census and the loss of status (2:28; 4:14) as a coded protest against the Augustan census of Egypt, which counted those who paid the poll tax and lowered the standing of many Jews; Tcherikover saw in it the spirit of the national revolt then rising in Judea.

Ewald and later writers linked it with the crisis under the emperor Caligula, about AD 40, when the Jews of Alexandria were persecuted and the emperor tried to place his image in the Temple. Emmet replied that the book lacks that crisis's marks: the statue, the attacks on synagogues, and real suffering.

For the Orthodox churches that read it as Scripture, its first readers include the church: it teaches trust in God's providence under hostile rulers, the power of the prayer of a priest, and God's care for the Temple and his people.

outline: Raphia: Theodotus's plot foiled by Dositheus, Arsinoe rallies the troops, the victory and the king's tour of the cities
The king at the Temple insists on entering the sanctuary; the priests, the city and its young women cry out
The prayer of Simon the high priest
God shakes the king and he is carried out
The pillar in Alexandria: sacrifice, census, the ivy-leaf brand, citizenship for initiates; most Jews refuse
Slander against the Jews; the Greeks of the city sympathize
The king's first letter: the Jews of Egypt to be brought in chains
Mourning everywhere; the deportation by ship to Schedia and the hippodrome
The registration fails: papyrus and pens run out
Drugged elephants; the king sleeps, then forgets
The third order; the Jews' last cry
Two angels; the elephants turn on the army
The king turns; seven days of feasting and the festival
The punishment of the Jews who had abandoned the Law
The return home, the pillar and place of prayer at Ptolemais, and the closing blessing

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern Orthodox churches read 3 Maccabees in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint, among the books outside the Hebrew canon: a story of God's providence over his Temple and his people far from it, of the power of priestly prayer, and of faithfulness under a hostile ruler.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 3 Maccabees as a Greek story written by an Alexandrian Jew in the late Ptolemaic or early Roman period, using the history of Ptolemy IV freely, perhaps joined with a later elephant story, to speak to the Jews of Egypt about loyalty, citizenship and God's rescue.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 3 Maccabees is not in the Jewish Bible and left no trace among the rabbis, but it shows how the Jews of Egypt saw themselves: loyal to the king, faithful to the Law, rescued by God, and keeping a festival of their own, as Purim was kept for Esther's rescue.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study the world of the first Christians: Jews of the Diaspora under a pagan ruler, slander and the charge of disloyalty, a mark that buys a place in society, prayer, angels and rescue, much as the church in Acts and Revelation would meet them.

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers: a Jewish writing outside their Bibles, never known in the Latin West, read for its witness to Jewish faith and life in Egypt before Christ and tested against the Bible rather than read as the Bible.

sections.b:
Read it as a story told for a community, not as a court chronicle. It opens in the middle of real history, at the battle of Raphia (1:1-5), names real people (Ptolemy IV, his sister Arsinoe, Theodotus), and uses the true titles and formulas of the Ptolemaic court. But it quickly becomes a tale of reversals, told in long, ornate Greek. The king who wants to enter the holy place is laid on the floor (2:22). The census meant to doom the Jews runs out of papyrus (4:20). The elephants meant to trample them trample the army (6:21). The king who ordered the slaughter throws a feast for his victims and calls them "the sons of the Almighty, heavenly, living God" (6:28).

Read it in two halves that mirror each other. In Jerusalem, a king threatens the Temple, the people pray through the high priest Simon, and God strikes the king (1:8-2:24). In Egypt, the same king threatens the people, they pray through the priest Eleazar, and God sends his angels (2:25-6:21). Each prayer rehearses God's past rescues; each crisis ends with the king humbled. The lesson is that God guards both his house and his people, even far from the land.

Watch the book's names for God. It loves long strings of titles: "King of the heavens and Master of all creation, Holy One among the holy, the only Ruler, the Almighty" (2:2); "the Most Great God"; "the Most High God, who rules over all power" (7:9); "the Rescuer of Israel" (7:23). Emmet counted several titles found nowhere else in the Greek Old Testament. Notice too what is missing: there is no Messiah, no end of the world and no life after death in this book. Its hope is rescue now, in this life.

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Greek as printed by H. B. Swete (1912), who follows Codex Alexandrinus and gives the readings of Codex Venetus in his notes. Swete's printed text has no verse 2:1, the opening of Simon's prayer, which Brenton's English of 1851 has; the Plain supplies it, and the variant note there says what each witness has. Brenton was used to check the sense; the King James Version has no 3 Maccabees. The book's Greek is unusually difficult, with very long sentences and rare words, so the Plain breaks its periods into short sentences while keeping every clause. Key titles are kept the same throughout: "the Most Great God," "the Most High," "the census" for laographia (2:28), and "equal citizens" (2:30).

The title is a puzzle. Nothing in the book is about the Maccabees, and its story is set about fifty years before their revolt. The Catholic Encyclopedia suggested it got the name because, like the others, it tells of a persecution of the Jews. Emmet thought the title was probably not original and arose because the book stood next to the other books of Maccabees in the manuscripts. A more fitting name, Swete and Emmet note, may be the one it seems to have borne in some circles, Ptolemaica, "The Ptolemaic history," if that is what the list called the Synopsis of pseudo-Athanasius means by that word; Wendland and Thackeray thought it meant the Letter of Aristeas instead.

What history confirms. The battle of Raphia is real, and Polybius, writing in the 100s BC, tells it at length (Histories 5.79-86). He agrees with 3 Maccabees on the main lines: Ptolemy's sister Arsinoe was with him, the Aetolian Theodotus slipped into the camp at night to kill the king (5.81), Arsinoe rode along the lines with the king to rouse the troops (5.83-84), Ptolemy won, and afterward he took Raphia and the other towns, whose people honored him "with crowns, sacrifices, altars" (5.86). Compare 1:6-7, where the king tours the nearby cities and gives gifts to their shrines.

Where it differs. Polybius says Theodotus missed the king because Ptolemy slept in another tent, and that he killed the king's physician Andreas instead (5.81); he never mentions Dositheus. 3 Maccabees credits a renegade Jew, Dositheus son of Drimylus, with laying a stand-in in the tent (1:3). Emmet reports that a Dositheus son of Drimylus appears in a papyrus (Hibeh Papyrus 90) as the priest of Alexander in 222 BC. Polybius gives Ptolemy 73 elephants at Raphia (5.79) and says most of his African elephants fled from Antiochus's Indian ones (5.84); 3 Maccabees has the king command five hundred elephants in Alexandria (5:2). Polybius says nothing of a visit to Jerusalem.

The elephant story in Josephus. Josephus tells a very similar story about a later king, Ptolemy Physcon, who came to Alexandria after the death of his brother Philometor. When the Jewish generals Onias and Dositheus backed Queen Cleopatra against him, Physcon had the Jews of Alexandria exposed "naked and in bonds" to elephants made drunk for the purpose; the elephants turned on his friends instead, a terrible apparition warned the king, his concubine pleaded for the Jews, and "the Alexandrian Jews do with good reason celebrate this day" (Against Apion 2.53-55). Emmet and the Catholic Encyclopedia both connect the two stories. Emmet judged Josephus's version far more probable and thought the writer of 3 Maccabees moved it to Philopator's reign and joined it to a story about the Temple.

A fair summary. The setting, the names, the court language and the festival point to real memories, and Swete quotes J. P. Mahaffy that a feast kept by the Egyptian Jews at a fixed date "cannot be an invention." The story as told, with its drugged elephants, its sleeping and forgetting king, and its angels, is shaped to show God at work. Scholars range from "a very weak piece of fiction" (the Catholic Encyclopedia) to Emmet's view that each incident, stripped of its color, "is entirely credible and probably has some foundation in fact."

By the 200s BC Egypt had a large Jewish population. The Letter of Aristeas says that Ptolemy son of Lagus carried a hundred thousand Jews from Judea to Egypt, armed thirty thousand of them as garrison troops in the countryside and made many of the rest slaves, and that his successor set the slaves free (Aristeas 12-27). Josephus names two Jewish generals, Onias and Dositheus, who commanded a Ptolemaic army (Against Apion 2.49). In the cities they gathered in their own "places of prayer" (compare 7:20) and read the Law in Greek, the Septuagint.

Their standing in the city was a sore point. Full citizens of Alexandria had privileges that others lacked, and the census (laographia) sorted people into ranks for tax. That is the threat of 2:28-30: to be "put on the census rolls and reduced to the condition of household slaves," unless one joined the king's mystery rites and so became one of the "equal citizens" with the Alexandrians. The book's answer is that true Jews would pay money to escape the rolls rather than buy citizenship with worship of Dionysus (2:32), and that the king's offer was really a trap (3:21-23).

sections.h: 3 Maccabees beside Esther, 2 Maccabees and the Letter of Aristeas
sections.b:
Esther. The two stories share a pattern: a king is persuaded that one people, "kept apart" with laws "unlike any other people's" (Esther 3:8), is disloyal; he sends letters ordering their destruction; the plan is reversed; the Jews feast and found a yearly festival "from grief to joy and from mourning to a holiday" (Esther 9:22). 3 Maccabees has the same charge (3:4, 7), the same kind of decree (3:12-29) and counter-decree (7:1-9), and the same festival (6:36; 7:19). It is closest to the Greek Esther, whose Additions B and E give the full text of the king's two letters (see the variant notes at Esther 3:13 and Esther 8:12): in both books the second letter blames the king's advisers and calls the Jews children of the living God (compare 6:28; 7:6). But in 3 Maccabees there is no Esther or Mordecai; the rescue comes from prayer and from God directly.

2 Maccabees. The Temple scene recalls Heliodorus, who tried to seize the Temple treasury and was struck down by heavenly riders and two young men "very beautiful in their glory" (2 Maccabees 3:24-29), just as Philopator is shaken to the floor (2:21-24) and two glorious angels come down at the hippodrome (6:18). Emmet listed the shared ideas (the holiness of the Temple, God's appearances, an aged Eleazar, royal letters, feasts of remembrance) and many rare words found in both books and nowhere else in the Greek Old Testament, but he thought the link was of school and period, not copying.

The Letter of Aristeas. This Alexandrian Jewish writing, in no church's Bible, also centers on a Ptolemy who honors the God of the Jews. Its king issues a decree freeing Jewish slaves, with a reward for anyone who informs on those who disobey (Aristeas 22-25), a mirror image of 3:25-28, where the informer is rewarded for betraying Jews. Its writer says the Temple service fills one "with astonishment and indescribable wonder" (Aristeas 99), as Philopator is "struck by the earnest care and devotion" he saw (1:9). Both use the official greeting of royal letters (3:12; 7:1) and discuss Jewish separateness in food (3:4). Emmet saw them as works of the same school and age; but where Aristeas has its spokesman tell the king that the Jews worship the same God as other people, who call him by names such as Zeus or Dis (Aristeas 12-20), 3 Maccabees allows no such bridge.

3 Maccabees was copied in Codex Alexandrinus, the 400s-AD Bible that has all four books of Maccabees, and in Codex Venetus. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85), a church order of the late 300s that the Council in Trullo (692) received for the Eastern churches, count "of the Maccabees, three" among the books to be held "venerable and sacred." The Stichometry of Nicephorus lists it too, while the list in Codex Claromontanus names a fourth book of Maccabees. Emmet observed that every early witness is Eastern: the book was never in the Latin Bible and is on no Western list. Today the Greek and Russian Bibles include it among the books outside the Hebrew canon, and the Orthodox Study Bible (2008), which takes its order from the Church of Greece's Septuagint of 1928, prints it after 2 Maccabees. The canon page below gives each church's practice.

• Ptolemy IV Philopator, Greek king of Egypt, victor at Raphia in 217 BC. "Philopator" means "father-loving."
  • Antiochus III, the Seleucid king of Syria he defeated (1:1).
  • Arsinoe, the king's sister, who rallies the troops (1:4).
  • Theodotus, the officer who tried to kill the king (1:2); Dositheus son of Drimylus, a Jew who left the Law and saved the king (1:3).
  • Simon, the high priest who prays in 2:1-20.
  • Eleazar, an aged priest of the Egyptian countryside who prays in 6:1-15.
  • Hermon, the master of the elephants (5:1).
  • The Most Great God, one of the book's favorite titles for God (1:16; 3:11; 5:25).
  • The census (Greek laographia), the registration of people for tax and status (2:28; 4:14).
  • The ivy leaf, the sign of Dionysus, god of wine and of mystery rites, whose mark and rites the king imposed (2:29-30).
  • Schedia, the landing place near Alexandria where the ships brought the prisoners (4:11); the hippodrome, the racecourse in front of the city.
  • Pachon and Epiphi, Egyptian months (6:38).
  • Ptolemais, "Rose-Bearing," the town where the fleet waited (7:17).

spec.title: Claude's theory: the king who sleeps too much
spec.body: In Esther the turning point comes when "sleep ran away from the king" (Esther 6:1): a sleepless night leads Ahasuerus to read the records and honor Mordecai. 3 Maccabees seems to turn this motif inside out. Its rescue comes when God sends the king "a portion of sleep" (5:11) so heavy that he misses the hour, and then a forgetting so complete that he does not know what he ordered (5:27-28). My suggestion is that the writer, who knew the Esther story in some form (the decree, the counter-decree and the festival all follow it), used the king's sleep on purpose, as a playful reversal: in Esther God works through a king who cannot sleep, here through a king who cannot stay awake. I have not found this comparison in the scholarship I checked for this page, so it should be read as my own idea.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the census that cannot be finished
spec.body: The book's sharpest weapon against the Jews is a list: they are to be "registered name by name" (4:14). The list never gets made. After forty days, the scribes report that the Jews are too many to count, and that "even the papyrus and the reed pens they wrote with had already run out" (4:20). My suggestion is that a Jewish reader would hear in this the old promise that Abraham's offspring would be beyond counting, like the stars and the sand (Genesis 15:5; Genesis 22:17), and perhaps the warning of David's census (2 Samuel 24:1-10): God's people are not the king's to number. The writer calls the failure "the unconquerable providence" (4:21). If Tcherikover is right that the book protests a real census, the joke would have been sharpest for readers who had just stood in line to be counted. This is my own reading, built on the verses given.

prompts: The king struck down in the Temple (2:21-23)

Inside a stone temple court with a great veiled doorway, a Greek king in a diadem and purple cloak lies sprawled on the paving, limbs twisted, his bodyguards and courtiers rushing to drag him away; an old high priest in white robes kneels before the sanctuary with hands raised; behind, crowds of men, women and veiled young girls with dust on their hair fill the court, crying out.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

In a vast oval racecourse outside a Greek city, war elephants with armor and towers wheel around and charge back into ranks of soldiers; above, two tall shining angels stand in an opening in the sky, seen by the soldiers who cower; on the sand, crowds of bound Jewish families lie face down, an old priest kneeling with raised hands; a king in a chariot recoils in terror.

views: Yes, in the Old Testament, among the books outside the Hebrew canon. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85) list "of the Maccabees, three" among the books "venerable and sacred" for clergy and laity, and the Council in Trullo (692, canon 2) confirmed those eighty-five canons. The preface to the Apocrypha in the New Revised Standard Version says that the books up to and including 3 Maccabees are recognized as Scripture by the Greek and the Russian churches, and the Orthodox Study Bible prints it in the Old Testament. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named "the Maccabees" among the genuine parts of Scripture without giving a number, and the Orthodox Church in America speaks of "the Books of Maccabees" as part of its "longer canon."

Divided. A Coptic Orthodox diocese answers that the book "is not considered a canonical book by our church," though it may be read with that understanding. The Syriac and Armenian churches have long had it in their Bibles: Emmet reports a Syriac version in the Peshitta and an Armenian version found in most manuscripts of the Armenian Bible.
Not this book. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church's list of its books includes books of "Maccabees," but these are the Meqabyan, which are entirely different in content from the Greek books of Maccabees.

No. The Council of Trent (1546) defined "two books of the Machabees, the first and the second." The Catholic Encyclopedia says that of the four books of that name only the first and second are regarded by the church as canonical, and that 3 Maccabees "seems never to have been known to the Latins"; it was never in the Latin Vulgate.
No, and not even among the Apocrypha read in church: the list of Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles ends with the First and Second Books of Maccabees.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the books called Apocrypha "are no part of the Canon of the Scripture," to be used only as other human writings; 3 Maccabees is not even among the Apocrypha of the King James Version.

canon.summary: 3 Maccabees is read in the Old Testament of the Eastern Orthodox churches, among the books outside the Hebrew canon, and stands in the Syriac and Armenian Bibles. The Coptic and Ethiopian Orthodox churches do not count it as canonical, and it is not in the Catholic, Protestant or Jewish Bible; it was never known in the Latin West.
accepted_by: In the Old Testament, read from the Septuagint. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85, late 300s) count "of the Maccabees, three" and recommend Sirach for the young besides; the Council in Trullo (692, canon 2) confirmed the eighty-five canons, though it confirmed in the same breath other lists that lack this book (Laodicea, Carthage, Athanasius). The NRSV's preface to the Apocrypha says the books up to and including 3 Maccabees are recognized as Scripture by the Greek and the Russian churches, and that 4 Maccabees stands in an appendix to the Greek Bible. The Orthodox Study Bible (2008) prints 3 Maccabees in its Old Testament, in the order of the Church of Greece's Septuagint of 1928. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named "the Maccabees" among the genuine books without a number; the Orthodox Church in America calls these books its "longer canon."

Read in their Bibles: Emmet reports a free, expanded Syriac version in the Peshitta and an Armenian version, probably of AD 400-600, found in most manuscripts of the Armenian Bible. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Syrian church was the first to receive it. Wikipedia's survey lists the Armenian Apostolic Church, the Syriac Orthodox Church and the Assyrian Church of the East among the churches that include it.
Not canonical. The Coptic Orthodox Diocese of the Southern United States answers that the book "is not considered a canonical book by our church," though it may be read with that understanding.
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches
Not this book. Their list of books includes three books of "Maccabees," but these are the Meqabyan, entirely different in content from the Greek books.

Not Scripture. The Council of Trent (1546) defined "two books of the Machabees, the first and the second." The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the third and fourth books apocryphal and says the third "seems never to have been known to the Latins"; there is no Latin version, and it is not in the Vulgate.

Not Scripture, and not among the Apocrypha of Article VI, whose list ends with the First and Second Books of Maccabees. Modern ecumenical editions such as the NRSV print it in an expanded Apocrypha for readers of the Eastern churches.
Reformed, Lutheran and other Protestant churches

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha "are no part of the Canon of the Scripture." 3 Maccabees is not among the Apocrypha of the King James Version. Wikipedia notes that some Protestant groups, such as the Moravian Brethren, include it in their Apocrypha.

Not Scripture. It is not in the Hebrew Bible and left no trace in rabbinic writing. Josephus does not use it, though he tells a related elephant story about Ptolemy Physcon and a day the Alexandrian Jews kept for it (Against Apion 2.53-55). Emmet notes that every ancient reference to the book is by Christian writers.

provenance.b: The book was written in Greek, not translated: its long periods, poetic compounds and rare words have no Hebrew behind them. Emmet counted more than a hundred words not found elsewhere in the Greek Old Testament and about fourteen found nowhere else in Greek. Its knowledge of the Ptolemaic court, of Alexandria and the Egyptian countryside, its Egyptian month names (6:38) and its official formulas, which Emmet found matched in papyri of about 100 BC, point to an Alexandrian Jewish writer.

No ancient writer before the Christian lists mentions it. It cannot be later than AD 70, since the Temple still stands. Within that range there are three main views. (1) Late Ptolemaic, about 100-30 BC: Emmet, from the letter formulas and papyri, about 100 BC; Thackeray, about 80 BC; and, in the summary on Wikipedia, Elias Bickerman, Hugh Anderson and Sara Raup Johnson. (2) Early Roman, about 25-15 BC: Tcherikover argued that the census (laographia), which in Roman Egypt meant the poll tax, points to the census Augustus held to count the poll-tax payers; Moses Hadas and others agree. (3) Under Caligula, about AD 40: Ewald and later writers saw in it the crisis of the Alexandrian Jews under that emperor. The Catholic Encyclopedia thought the book knows the Greek Additions to Daniel and so is no earlier than the first century BC; Emmet likewise saw in 6:6 a quotation of the Greek Song of the Three Young Men.

The writer seems to have drawn on good knowledge of Philopator's reign: his account of Raphia agrees in outline with Polybius but has details Polybius lacks, such as Dositheus (1:3) and Arsinoe's promise of two minas of gold (1:4). Emmet suggested a lost history of the reign by Ptolemy of Megalopolis, who wrote anecdotes about Philopator's court and his drinking companions. The elephant story has a parallel in Josephus under Ptolemy Physcon (Against Apion 2.53-55), and Emmet thought the writer joined that later story to an earlier Temple story.

The Greek survives in Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), the only great early codex with all four books of Maccabees, and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), and in a few later manuscripts, some of which give a Lucianic text. Codex Vaticanus has no books of Maccabees; Codex Sinaiticus has 1 and 4 Maccabees but not 2 or 3. Swete printed Alexandrinus with Venetus in his notes. Emmet found the text "generally well preserved": the variants seldom change the sense and usually try to simplify the writer's forced phrasing. Swete's printed text lacks verse 2:1, which Brenton's English has.

A free Syriac version stands in the Peshitta, and an Armenian version was made, Emmet reports, probably between AD 400 and 600. There is no Latin. The book appears in the Apostolic Canons (canon 85), the Stichometry of Nicephorus, and probably in the Synopsis of pseudo-Athanasius under the name Ptolemaica. Theodoret summarized it in his commentary on Daniel 11 and treated it as history, and Swete noted (as Emmet reports) that the Liturgy of St. Clement joins words of Isaiah 57:15 with the opening of Simon's prayer (2:2). Every one of these witnesses is Eastern.

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b: Its two prayers retell the Bible's rescues. Simon recalls the giants and the Flood (2:4; Genesis 6:4; Genesis 7:21-23), Sodom (2:5; Genesis 19:24-25), Pharaoh and the sea (2:6-7; Exodus 14), the choice of Jerusalem for God's name (2:9; Deuteronomy 12:5) and Solomon's prayer that God would hear his people when they turn and pray toward the house (2:10; 1 Kings 8:33-34). Eleazar recalls Pharaoh (6:4), Sennacherib (6:5; 2 Kings 19:35), the three in the furnace (6:6; Daniel 3), Daniel in the lions' den (6:7; Daniel 6) and Jonah (6:8; Jonah 2), and he quotes God's promise not to overlook his people in the land of their enemies (6:15; compare Leviticus 26:44). The rule that only the high priest may enter the sanctuary, once a year (1:11), is the law of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 34). The plot, decree and festival follow the pattern of Esther.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: 3 Maccabees was never in the Hebrew Bible, was written in Greek, probably in the last century BC or later, and left no trace in rabbinic writing. Josephus does not use it (Emmet). Protestants argue in their strongest form that the Old Testament the church received from Israel is the Hebrew Bible, the books Jesus and the apostles called the Scriptures (Romans 3:2).

rejected_why.h: It was never known in the West
rejected_why.b: Unlike 1 and 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees never reached the Latin church. There is no Latin version and it is on no Western list (Swete; Emmet), so it was never in the Vulgate. For Catholics the question was settled at Trent, which named two books of Maccabees, the first and the second; for Protestants it hardly arose, because the book was not in the Latin Bible they inherited, nor among the Apocrypha of Article VI or of the King James Version.

Even in the East the witness is mixed. The Apostolic Canons list three books of Maccabees, but the Council in Trullo, which confirmed those canons, confirmed in the same canon other lists that do not include 3 Maccabees, such as those of Laodicea and Athanasius. The Coptic Orthodox Church today says the book is not canonical, and Ethiopian Bibles have other books of "Maccabees."

The book tells real people's names in a story that most historians think did not happen as told. Its elephant story has a closer parallel under a later king in Josephus (Against Apion 2.53-55). Its five hundred elephants (5:2), its census that runs out of papyrus (4:20), and its king who forgets in a night what he ordered (5:27-28) belong to the art of the tale. The Catholic Encyclopedia judged that it "abounds in absurdities and psychological impossibilities"; the Cambridge Bible on Revelation called it "stupid as it is," though it allowed that it "has perhaps some historical foundation." On this view a book whose story is so freely told cannot be the Word of God, however true its faith.

The book ends with the faithful Jews asking the king's leave to kill those who had abandoned the Law "for the sake of their stomachs" (7:11), and receiving it "without needing any royal authority or review" (7:12). "On that day they killed more than three hundred men, and they kept it as a day of joy and gladness" (7:15). The Law of Moses did command death for one who led others to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6-10; Deuteronomy 17:2-5), but only after the matter was looked into "with care" and on the word of two or three witnesses: "He must not be put to death on the word of one witness" (Deuteronomy 17:6). And the New Testament says, "never take revenge yourselves" (Romans 12:19). Readers in every tradition have found these verses hard; for those who do not hold the book as Scripture, they are one more reason not to.

The Orthodox do not rest the book's place on a council like Trent. They point to the Septuagint the church has always read, to the Apostolic Canons and their reception at Trullo, and to long use in the Greek, Russian, Syriac and Armenian Bibles. They read the book for what it teaches: trust in God under a hostile ruler, the power of prayer, and God's care for his people far from Jerusalem. Reading it among the books outside the Hebrew canon also leaves Orthodox readers room to treat its story as a story and its hard ending as the record of a deed, not a model.

cited_in.b: The beast from the land makes everyone "be given a mark on their right hand or on their forehead" (Revelation 13:16), so that no one can buy or sell without it (Revelation 13:17). 3 Maccabees tells of a king who ordered every Jew enrolled in the census to have "the mark of Dionysus, an ivy leaf, burned into his body" (2:29), and who offered equal citizenship to any who joined the mystery rites (2:30): a pagan mark as the price of a place in society. Commentators on Revelation point to it: the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges on Revelation 13:16 cites the ivy-leaf brand of Ptolemy Philopator, and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown cite 2:29 (beside 2 Maccabees 6:7). John names no book, and branding for a god was known widely; the link is to a shared idea, not a quotation.

Paul says, "I am carrying the marks of Jesus in my own body" (Galatians 6:17), using the Greek word for brands (stigmata). The Pulpit Commentary on that verse, gathering ancient examples of branding, cites 2:29, where Jews were to have the mark of Dionysus burned into their bodies, though it judges that this was meant as an insult more than as making them the god's slaves. A background example, not a source Paul used.

Hebrews says the inner tent "is entered by the high priest alone, once a year" (Hebrews 9:7), from the law of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 34). The priests tell Philopator the same rule: no Gentile may go in, nor all the priests, "only the high priest, who leads them all, and he only one time each year" (1:11). Both reflect the Temple practice of their day; Hebrews does not cite 3 Maccabees.

Hebrews' list of the faithful who "shut lions' mouths" (Hebrews 11:33) and "put out the power of fire" (Hebrews 11:34) points to Daniel and the three young men (Daniel 6; Daniel 3). Eleazar's prayer makes the same pair the proof that God rescues his people (6:6-7). The link is a shared way of telling Israel's history, not dependence; both draw on Daniel.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt believed and felt before Jesus, 3 Maccabees is valuable: it shows their loyalty to the Ptolemies and to the Temple in Jerusalem, their pain at being slandered as disloyal and separate, the pressure to buy citizenship with pagan worship, their trust in prayer, and a festival of their own. As a text it is well preserved in Greek, its original language, though in only two early codices and with a gap at 2:1 in Swete's printed text. As history it is weak: the setting at Raphia is real and agrees in outline with Polybius, and its court language is accurate, but the story of the elephants is told about another king by Josephus, and the drugged beasts, the census that runs out of papyrus and the angels are shaped to show God at work. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their faith in the one God who guards his people and hears prayer, says nothing of a Messiah or the life to come, and in its ending, the killing of the apostates without trial, sits uneasily with the Law's own demand for inquiry and witnesses.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish life in Egypt: high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. The book shows Jews of Egypt who keep apart in food and worship (3:4, 7) yet insist they are the king's most loyal subjects (3:3; 5:31; 6:25-26); who feel the sting of the charge that they are enemies of the state (3:7, 24); who face a census that would make them "household slaves" (2:28) and an offer of citizenship at the price of the Dionysus rites (2:30); who split between those who gave in and those who paid to stay off the rolls (2:31-33); and who pray in long strings of titles for God (2:2; 6:2) and keep a festival for their rescue (6:36; 7:19). It is one of the clearest pictures of Diaspora Jewish life before the New Testament, the world from which Paul's Greek-speaking synagogues came.

Well. The Greek is the original. It survives in Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD) and Codex Venetus (700s AD) and a few later manuscripts, with a Syriac and an Armenian version as further witnesses. Emmet found the text "generally well preserved," its variants seldom affecting the sense. The one gap that matters for this site is 2:1, missing from Swete's printed text; the variant note there gives what each witness has. No early Jewish writer quotes it; every ancient reference to it is Christian (Emmet).

What fits. The battle of Raphia, Arsinoe's presence, Theodotus's night attack on the king's tent and the king's tour of the conquered towns all agree with Polybius (Histories 5.79-86). A Dositheus son of Drimylus is known from a papyrus of 222 BC (as Emmet reports), and Emmet found the book's official words, letter formulas and census terms matched in Ptolemaic papyri.

What does not. Polybius has Theodotus kill the physician Andreas, not a stand-in placed by a Jew (5.81), and says nothing of Jerusalem. Ptolemy had 73 elephants at Raphia (5.79); the book's five hundred (5:2) look like storytelling. The elephant scene is told by Josephus about a later king, Ptolemy Physcon (Against Apion 2.53-55), with the same drunk elephants, the same turning of the beasts and the same yearly day. Emmet thought the writer moved the story to Philopator, and that the Temple visit and the Egyptian persecution were joined by him; the book itself never explains why an insult in Jerusalem should turn the king against the Jews of Egypt.

The answer of those who hold it. The Orthodox churches have made no ruling on these questions that we could find; their reading stresses what the story teaches. Emmet, though no defender of its every detail, thought each incident, without its color, "entirely credible," and Swete quotes Mahaffy that a feast kept on a fixed date "cannot be an invention." A fair summary: real names and a real setting, an old tradition of a rescue that Alexandrian Jews remembered, and a story told freely to show God's care.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: the one God, Creator and King, who judges the proud (2:2-5; Psalm 2:4; Daniel 4:37); the holiness of the sanctuary, entered only by the high priest once a year (1:11; Leviticus 16:2, 34; Hebrews 9:7); God's choice of Jerusalem and his promise to hear prayer made toward his house (2:9-10; 1 Kings 8:29-30, 33-34); rescue through prayer, as with Hezekiah and Daniel (6:5-7; 2 Kings 19:15-35; Daniel 6); angels sent to defend God's people (6:18; 2 Kings 6:17; Psalm 34:7); loyalty to a pagan ruler without worshiping his gods (3:3-4; Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 3:16-18); God's humbling of a proud king (2:21-22; Daniel 4:31-33).
  • Goes beyond: (a) a new festival not in the Law, like Purim (6:36; 7:19; Esther 9:20-28); (b) angels "who could be seen by everyone except the Jews" (6:18), a detail with no parallel in the 66 books; (c) God's sending sleep and forgetting to the king as means of rescue (5:11-12, 27-28), an image of providence the Bible hints at (Esther 6:1; Proverbs 21:1) but never tells this way.
  • Leaves out: any Messiah, any hope of resurrection or judgment after death; Emmet noted there is no messianic hope or future life in the book. Its hope is rescue now.
  • May conflict: (a) the killing of the apostates (7:10-15): more than three hundred Jews put to death on the road, "without needing any royal authority or review" (7:12), and the day kept with joy. The Law required careful inquiry and two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:4-6), and Paul forbids private revenge (Romans 12:19). (b) A severe line toward those who gave in (2:33): the faithful shut them out of every kind of help, where the prophets also call the straying back (Ezekiel 18:30-32).
  • Each church's view: the Orthodox read the book with the rest of their Old Testament as a witness to God's providence, its hard ending as a narrated deed; Catholics and Protestants read it as a human Jewish writing, valuable background, never a rule of faith.

how_to_read.b: If you are Eastern Orthodox, 3 Maccabees is in your Old Testament, among the books read beside the Hebrew ones, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide. If you are Catholic or Protestant, it is not in your Bible, and it never was; read it as an ancient Jewish story, like the Letter of Aristeas. If you are Coptic or Ethiopian Orthodox, your church does not count it either.

how_to_read.h: Read it as a story with a lesson
how_to_read.b: Do not expect a chronicle. Expect a tale of reversals, told in heavy, ornate Greek, about a God who guards his Temple and his people. Notice how the king's plans fail one after another, and how the writer keeps saying who is behind it: "the unconquerable providence" (4:21), "the working of God" (5:28).

how_to_read.h: Read it beside Esther, Daniel and 2 Maccabees
how_to_read.b: Read Esther 3 and 8-9 beside chapters 3, 6 and 7, and the Greek Additions B and E in the variant notes at Esther 3:13 and Esther 8:12. Read Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 with Eleazar's prayer (6:6-7). Read 2 Maccabees 3, the story of Heliodorus, beside 1:8-2:24.

The charge against the Jews here, that they keep strange customs and are disloyal to the ruler (3:7), is the kind of charge brought against Paul and Silas at Philippi (Acts 16:20-21), and the community of Greek-speaking Jews it describes is the one the apostles first preached to (Acts 2:10; Acts 6:9). The book helps a reader see that world from the inside.

Read 7:10-15 honestly. The writer celebrates the killing of three hundred Jews who had given up the Law. Set it beside the Law's demand for inquiry and witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:4-6) and beside the gospel's call to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19), and decide for yourself what the story approves and what it only reports.
